vignette:
Layla

Layla was thirty-eight when her mother died, and it was only then that she allowed herself to remember clearly what her mother had done. For twenty-five years before that—from age five until she left home at thirteen—her mother had used her as a vessel for rage. The punishments came without warning. A spilled glass of milk, a tone of voice misread, a day when her mother had simply decided that Layla's existence was an affront. The smell of arak on her mother's breath had become the herald of violence; Layla learned to track that scent the way an animal tracks a predator. Her mother would give orders—stand still, don't cry, apologize—and when Layla's small body inevitably failed to obey perfectly, the belt came, or her mother's hands. The messages were clear and relentless: Layla was the problem. Layla deserved it. Layla could have prevented it if she had only been better, faster, quieter, more compliant. By the time she left for college, Layla had internalized a profound conviction: she was fundamentally unable to protect herself, and nothing she did would ever be enough to stop bad things from happening to her.

She built a careful life after that. She became a pharmacist—a role that gave her authority without requiring her to submit to it, a position of precision and control. She married Ahmed, a gentle man who asked little and gave steadily. For years, the past remained compartmentalized, a locked room she did not enter. But at forty-three, after her mother's funeral, Layla found that room had broken open.

The first break came at work. Her pharmacy manager, a woman named Patricia, began implementing new protocols and issuing directives in the clipped, authoritative tone that Layla's nervous system had learned to recognize as dangerous. Being given orders or instructions—even routine ones about inventory or scheduling—triggered an immediate cascade. Layla's body would flood with the certainty that she was in danger, that something terrible was about to happen, even though she was standing in a fluorescent-lit pharmacy in 2024. The false alarms came relentlessly. When Patricia called her into the office to discuss workflow improvements, Layla's heart raced as if she were five years old again, waiting for the blow. She found herself unable to concentrate on the actual words being spoken; instead, her mind fractured into fragments of vigilance. She had to stay alert. She had to monitor Patricia's posture, her tone, the distance between them. Sleep became impossible—she would lie awake beside Ahmed, her body coiled, certain that if she let her guard down something catastrophic would occur.

The memories, when they surfaced, felt more real and vivid than anything happening in the present moment. She could smell the arak. She could feel the specific texture of the fabric of her mother's dress. These sensations were not faint echoes; they were immediate, overwhelming, more present than her own marriage, her own achievement. When the memories returned, she felt so consumed by emotion—by rage and terror and a helplessness so complete it seemed to erase her—that she had to stop whatever she was doing. Sometimes she would sit in her car in the pharmacy parking lot and simply weep. Other times the feeling would vanish entirely and she would recall the events with a strange, clinical numbness, as if she were reading about something that had happened to someone else entirely, which was almost worse because it made her feel like a fraud, like she was overreacting to nothing.

The smell of alcohol became a particular torment. Ahmed occasionally had wine with dinner; a colleague wore cologne with an alcohol base; once, a customer spilled hand sanitizer near the register. Each time, Layla's threat system erupted. The smell would trigger the memory with brutal immediacy, and the memory would drag with it the conviction that she was helpless, that she had failed in every important role—as a daughter, as a wife, as a woman capable of building something safe. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore. Her marriage, her career, even her own survival seemed hollow, as if she had only been going through motions. The helplessness was the worst part. She had become a pharmacist, had learned to manage complex systems, had built a life of apparent competence—and yet she could not stop the terror from coming. She could not control her own nervous system.

To manage the unbearable weight of the memories and the certainty of danger, Layla began to hurt herself. She would pinch the soft skin on her inner arm until it bruised, or hold ice against her wrist until it burned. The physical pain interrupted the intrusive memories; it gave her something immediate and controllable to focus on. When she felt the false alarms rising—the sense that danger was imminent even in her safe home—she would scratch at her cuticles until they bled. The pain was a kind of relief, a way of stopping the thinking, stopping the overwhelming emotion. But the self-harm also deepened her sense of failure. She was harming herself. She was weak. She was the problem.

She began to avoid situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful. Ahmed suggested a weekend trip; she declined, citing work. Her sister invited her to a baby shower; Layla made an excuse. She could not bear the vulnerability of joy, the risk that something good might be taken away. She stopped attending the pharmacy's social events, then stopped going to her mosque, then stopped calling friends. She avoided any setting where there might be authority figures—uniforms, hierarchies, people with power over her. The avoidance itself became a trigger, a way of reinforcing her belief that the world was dangerous, that she was right to be afraid, that she could not be safe anywhere. Each time she declined an invitation or left a room when a supervisor entered, she told herself it was the smart choice. It was survival. But it was also a kind of slow disappearance.

By the time Ahmed finally insisted she see someone, Layla had become almost unrecognizable to the people who loved her. She was present in her home but absent from her life. She moved through her shifts at the pharmacy with mechanical efficiency, avoiding Patricia, avoiding eye contact, avoiding anything that might demand that she be fully present. She had lost weight. She had dark circles under her eyes from the vigilant insomnia. What frightened her most was the possibility that this—this hollow, terrified, self-harming version of herself—was who she had always been underneath, and that her years of functioning had been a kind of elaborate illusion. She came to therapy because Ahmed gave her an ultimatum, but what she was most hoping for, though she barely dared to articulate it, was to feel like herself again—or perhaps, for the first time, to feel like a self at all.
